reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: An inherited, usually autosomal recessive disorder of ciliary structure and function that impairs mucociliary clearance throughout the respiratory tract
Presents from early life with chronic wet cough, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic rhinosinusitis, and glue ear leading to bronchiectasis
Unexplained neonatal respiratory distress in a term infant is an important early clue often overlooked in retrospect
Roughly half of patients have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome comprises bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and situs inversus) because embryonic nodal cilia determine organ laterality
A very low nasal nitric oxide level is a useful screening pointer in older children and adults
Diagnosis is supported by high-speed video microscopy of ciliary beat, electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure, and genetic testing
Management centres on airway clearance, prompt treatment of infections, and surveillance of lung function, mirroring principles used in bronchiectasis
Male infertility and reduced female fertility are common because sperm flagella and fallopian tube cilia share the same defect
reference.pathophysiology: Primary ciliary dyskinesia arises from mutations in any of numerous genes encoding components of the motile cilium (such as dynein arms and other axonemal proteins), producing cilia that beat abnormally or not at all. Defective mucociliary clearance leads to stasis of secretions, chronic bacterial infection, and progressive airway damage culminating in bronchiectasis and chronic rhinosinusitis. Because motile cilia also govern left-right body axis determination during embryogenesis, laterality defects such as situs inversus occur, and dysfunction of the structurally related sperm flagellum and oviduct cilia impairs fertility.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable and other primary immunodeficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Nasal nitric oxide measurement as a screening test
High-speed video microscopy to assess ciliary beat frequency and pattern
Transmission electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure
Genetic testing for known PCD-associated mutations
High-resolution CT to define and monitor bronchiectasis
Sputum microbiology and immunological workup to exclude alternative diagnoses
redFlags: Severe or recurrent lower respiratory infection with clinical deterioration
Rapidly progressive decline in lung function suggesting advancing bronchiectasis
Massive or recurrent haemoptysis from established bronchiectasis
Signs of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: With coordinated care many patients maintain reasonable lung function into adulthood, but recurrent infection can cause progressive bronchiectasis and, in some, respiratory failure; life expectancy is generally better than in cystic fibrosis.
pitfalls: Dismissing chronic productive cough in a child as recurrent simple infections and delaying diagnosis
Assuming absence of situs inversus excludes the disorder, since only about half of patients have it
Relying on a single test rather than combining nasal nitric oxide, microscopy, and genetics
Failing to address fertility, ENT, and hearing issues as part of multisystem care
